what: the key to the relation test's readings files and the PI's two sheets: for nobody, and not for the PI until the coders' replies are in

citations.bechky: Bechky, B. A. 2020. Evaluative spillovers from technological change: The effects of "DNA envy" on occupational practices in forensic science. Administrative Science Quarterly, 65(3): 606–643.
citations.pratt: Pratt, M. G. 2000. The good, the bad, and the ambivalent: Managing identification among Amway distributors. Administrative Science Quarterly, 45(3): 456–493.

readings.text: Narcotics analysts' resistance could primarily be a defense of a workable production system under legal deadlines and limited equipment. A technique can be available and scientifically acceptable without being feasible for the entire caseload. Read this way, the contrast with toxicology reflects the unequal costs and scale of the requested changes: toxicology added calculations to established work, while narcotics faced replacing its main route through a heavy workload. Occupational preferences would reinforce this difference without necessarily causing it. Narcotics analysts already used GC/MS for unfamiliar substances or drugs unsuitable for crystal testing (p. 629). They nevertheless relied on rapid crystal tests for common cases because local law imposed short turnaround times. This distinguishes resistance to universal deployment from rejection of instrumentation itself. Analysts contested delays introduced by a new reporting system and discussed differences measured in minutes (p. 631). This shows that small processing costs mattered in everyday work even when DNA comparisons were not the immediate issue. An analyst explained that two available instruments and lengthy runs could not accommodate the caseload (p. 632). The proposed second examination of crystals would require repeating the tests, while microscope cameras were discussed as a less expensive alternative to more GC/MS instruments. These passages identify concrete capacity constraints and possible remedies. Toxicology's revised reporting drew on established equipment, methods, and accumulated data (p. 628). This supplies a comparison in which the change could build on existing capacity rather than displace the main production method.

Compatibility is settled inside one laboratory, one facet at a time, not between a method and DNA profiling. The pathway picks the facet—error measurement, instrument output, population statistics—and the lab's instruments, records, protocols and statutes decide whether it can be met at scale. Toxicology adapted because its quality-control history, traceability log and mandated confidence interval had already paid for the change. Narcotics held a compatible method, but two instruments, long runs and a statutory charging clock kept it off routine cases. Firearms, already imaging their striae, were incompatible only on the facet the critics chose. Feasibility is where a method meets a budget and a clock. DNA profiling meant something different to each group: an overarching statistical practice for firearms, error measurement for toxicology, the certainty of instrument output for narcotics (p. 634). Compatibility was tested not against the whole benchmark but against the facet each pathway made salient, which is the hinge of the reading. GC/MS's logs and graphs were seen in the narcotics community as matching DNA standards, yet at MCCL crystal tests carried most cases because the jurisdiction's law demanded rapid turnaround for charging and methamphetamine could be confirmed by crystals in minutes (pp. 628–629). Establishes both the compatible method and the statutory clock under which it had to perform. Robin says the lab could not keep up with its caseload without crystals, having two instruments with long runs; the unit notes a second-analyst review would double analysis time and weighs microscope cameras as far cheaper than more GC/MS instruments (p. 632). Instrument count, caseload and budget are the decisive terms, and the unit pursued adaptation along the facet it could afford. Toxicology already had an ISO plan for uncertainty of measurement, a protocol logging instruments and standards, a state-mandated confidence interval, and five years of quality-control data from an unchanged instrument, from which Jason assembled the new figure (pp. 627–628). Its compatibility was a stock of prior mandates, routines and records that had absorbed most of the cost before the challenge arrived. Examiners build note packets of digital images over several days and recount that sight-based identification is no longer acceptable now that images are required (pp. 621–622). Firearms had already met an earlier objectifying demand once imaging equipment and documentation norms were in place; their incompatibility is specific to the statistical facet the critics selected.

The three responses follow what change would cost each unit in instruments, staff time and legal deadlines. Values are the language in which those costs are expressed. Toxicology changed because the change was nearly free: the data existed and the method stayed the same. Narcotics held on to crystal tests because the unit could not meet its statutory turnaround with two instruments. Firearms did nothing because nothing affordable was on offer: no population data exist for a four-person unit to report from. Local law required fast turnaround on drug cases, and the commonest drug could be confirmed by crystal test in ten to fifteen minutes (p. 629). This sets a hard throughput constraint. An analyst says the unit could not keep up with its caseload without crystals because it has only two instruments and runs are long (p. 632). The objection is stated as capacity, not preference. Second-analyst review would double analysis time, and cameras are discussed as costly but cheaper than more instruments (p. 632). The unit is pricing alternatives, which is what a cost-driven actor does. The veteran analyst's objection to instrument testing is that it takes much longer and results would not come back at once (p. 631). Speed leads her account. Analysts time themselves and fight a new data-entry system over a minute per case, which shows how tightly throughput governs the unit (p. 631). Toxicology's new reporting reused existing historical data, the same instrument and the same method, so adoption required little new resource (pp. 627–628). Other units remark that equipment, funding, grants and staff flow to the DNA unit (p. 619). The resources that would make being like DNA possible sit elsewhere. Firearms examiners say statistics are impossible because not every bullet can be examined, which is a statement about missing data infrastructure (p. 624).

The apparent coherence of occupational values could partly be produced by people sorting themselves into work they already prefer. In particular, narcotics may collect analysts who dislike repetitive instrument work and leave units where that work predominates. Resistance would then express the preferences of a selected local membership as well as values learned through practicing an occupation. On this reading, job movement helps create the cultural differences that the paper subsequently uses to explain responses to evaluation. Several narcotics analysts had previously worked in toxicology and wanted to leave (p. 630). One described entering toxicology because it had a vacancy, then persuading management to provide training elsewhere because the balance of paperwork and benchwork was unsatisfactory. This is direct evidence of dissatisfaction preceding a move into the unit whose values it later exemplified. Criminalists entered with broadly similar educational backgrounds and were hired into particular units (p. 613). This establishes a common recruitment pool from which initial placement and subsequent movement could generate differences between unit memberships. The laboratory regarded criminalists as potentially interchangeable across units, and the director was planning a transfer involving narcotics and firearms (p. 619). This shows that the boundaries treated analytically as occupational were also crossed through organizational staffing decisions. A narcotics analyst explicitly recognized that other people preferred instrument-based routines while she preferred varied chemical work (p. 632). This permits a reading in which divergent individual preferences help determine where workers settle.

Re-attribute what separated the two units, from fit with what each values to how much of the unit's routine the change would displace and what that would cost. On the toxicology side the change in print is to the report and the calculation behind it. Toxicology as the paper observed it was high-volume instrument work (p. 625). The protocol already logged instruments, reagents and standards, and the laboratory had been reporting at a 95% confidence level (p. 627). The courtroom attack was on reports that omitted measurement-uncertainty estimates (p. 625); the unit prepared the statistical analysis on a plan it already had (p. 627), and the new calculation used several years of existing quality-control data (pp. 627–628). No passage prints a change to how samples are prepared or run. On the narcotics side what the analysts feared losing was the routine bench method: they feared their working group might eventually prohibit crystal testing (p. 631). Crystal tests handled many routine cases and often confirmed common methamphetamine in about ten to fifteen minutes, GC/MS was reserved for unknown or unconfirmed substances, and rapid legal turnaround made the faster method especially useful (p. 629). Robin said the laboratory could not handle its caseload without crystals because it had only two relevant instruments and instrument runs took too long (p. 632). Jodi expected a shift toward slower GC/MS if crystal testing were phased out (p. 631). The analysts said a rule of independent visual confirmation would in effect require a fresh duplicate test and roughly double the work (p. 632), and they noted that microscope cameras would cost less than additional GC/MS instruments (p. 632). So the two instrument-based routes the pair holds comparable are not the same size of thing. For toxicology the instrument method was the routine and the demand added a calculation to it. For narcotics the instrument method was the exception, and what the analysts feared would have put it in place of the routine. The wager is that this difference, in how much of the day's work is displaced and what that costs in instruments and time against the caseload, is what made the units come out differently, and that the values the paper credits accompany each outcome without being shown to produce it. Two things in print lean this way. The narcotics analysts' stated reasons divide: time, work and cost in the passages on p. 631 and p. 632; variety and what the work asks of the analyst in the passages on p. 632. That they were especially troubled by the second kind is the author's account (p. 632). And on the toxicology side the participant passages show vigilance against sample-identity and pipetting mistakes (p. 626, pp. 626–627); the fit between that and estimating uncertainty across equipment, reagents and procedural steps (pp. 627–628) is made in the author's voice (p. 627; Table 2, Values — toxicology, p. 633), and the nearest participant-side item is pride shown when the new reports were presented (p. 628), which comes after the change. The reading is close to the paper in one respect: the paper's own account of narcotics values includes quick case completion (p. 630, p. 631, author's account), so speed is registered. It parts from the paper in treating instruments, run time and caseload as conditions of the laboratory, not as something the analysts value, and in crediting them for the outcome where the paper's claim (p. 628, p. 632, pp. 633–637) credits variety, autonomy and craft judgment.

The firearms unit had already met the demand in the form comparison microscopy can carry. It replaced claims of personal recognition with an image-by-image record, countersigned by a second examiner and built to be reviewed by outsiders and to hold up on the stand; that is the reviewable-record part of the DNA model. What it refuses is the statistical part alone. Read this way, 'never been challenged' is what earlier adaptation looks like from inside, and the units differ in which piece of the DNA model each could take up, and when, more than in embracing or resisting it. Forensic biologists built their ways of presenting evidence as DNA was challenged in court; the legal parties can inspect the raw data, graphs and tables; yet the analysts regard the work behind them as messy judgment settled among colleagues (pp. 618–619). Seen from inside, the DNA model is judgment made reviewable for court, which is the part a firearms unit could take. The image record exists to back judgments on the stand; packets hold images of every compared set, matching or not; a senior examiner says outsiders have reviewed his work [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 621]' (p. 621). The absence of local challenge can then be credited to the record. Examiners say appeals to personal recognition are no longer accepted in reports or testimony and that images are now required; a second examiner views each comparison and signs each page (p. 622). This is the change itself, with the examiners' stated reason. All three qualified examiners are trained in the counting method and one keeps it for borderline calls (p. 623). The numerical route is held in reserve. An examiner at the statewide meeting, drawing on questioning by defense attorneys, says critics build on examiners' own testimony and that it falls to examiners to be more convincing (pp. 623–624). Members of the discipline treat courtroom demand as a reason to improve the record, the motive the unit gives for its images. Toxicologists met the demand narrowly, as one standard on measurement error (p. 627). This is the paper's own precedent for a unit taking a single part of the DNA model. Narcotics analysts weigh microscope cameras and a second viewer for crystal tests, whose exposure (p. 631) is that they leave nothing to review later (p. 632). Reviewability is the DNA-like quality at stake in this lab; firearms already has it.

Re-attribute what separated the two units. The paper credits distance: remote for firearms, immediate for toxicology. A second thing varied across the pair and is printed on one side only: a change already being worked toward under a standing requirement. Before the NAS report the laboratory was adapting to ISO 17025 and the toxicology unit had a multi-year plan to estimate measurement uncertainty (p. 627). State law and ASCLD required a five-percent confidence range for blood-alcohol measurement, the protocol already logged instruments, reagents and standards, and the laboratory was reporting at a 95% confidence level while preparing fuller uncertainty estimates for ISO compliance (p. 627). When the local challenge became imminent the unit accelerated that plan and prepared the statistical analysis (p. 627). At an outreach session for criminal-justice personnel Jason rejected the idea that the laboratory had only begun uncertainty work because of the NAS report, cited ISO and NIST requirements, and said the new calculation used several years of existing quality-control data (pp. 627–628). The paper's own table puts ASCLD accreditation standards in toxicology's professional-association cell (Table 2, Professional association — toxicology, p. 633, author's account) and identifies no professional-association route for firearms (Table 2, Professional association — firearms, p. 633, author's account). On the firearms side no passage prints a plan for the unit, and none says what the laboratory's ISO 17025 adaptation (p. 627) asked of it. The one professional-body response printed on the firearms criticism is a rebuttal: AFTE leaders issued a detailed rebuttal to parts of the NAS criticism of firearms work (p. 623). IAI and AFTE also answered the report with selected rebuttals and commitments to have their research committees study the recommendations further (p. 616). One examiner's work, at least, had been under outside review: Adam says outsiders had repeatedly reviewed his work without challenging it (p. 621). Read this way, the pair does not set a unit that changed beside a unit that did not. It sets a unit whose change was already planned and required beside a unit with no plan and no requirement of its own in print, and the imminent challenge brought the plan forward. The wager is that the standing requirement is what made the difference, and that the immediate route accounts for when toxicology's reports changed, not for the fact that they did. A requirement met on a multi-year plan is hard to count among the paper's locally immediate routes (p. 606, p. 608, p. 617, p. 620, pp. 624–625, pp. 627–628, p. 632, pp. 633–636), so on this reading the pair shows the slower route doing the work. This sits close to the paper's claim (p. 625, pp. 627–628, pp. 633–637), which already lists accreditation work under way, and to the passage on p. 635, where the author's account has that work making the change easier. It parts from the paper's claim (p. 606, p. 608, p. 617, p. 620, pp. 624–625, pp. 627–628, p. 632, pp. 633–636), which takes this pair to show that immediacy supplies the impetus.

Retold from the forensic biology unit's own passages, the paper's episode has no event in it. None of the unit's fourteen passages has a DNA analyst speak of the 2009 report, of being the standard, or of the other units; the nearest is the supervisors introducing themselves, as a joke, on the author's first day, as the 'DNA princesses' (p. 615). What the passages do carry is the unit's account of its own work and one line of history. At the bench the analysts regard profiling as judgment-laden and untidy, because instrument output can contain artifacts and samples can be dirty, degraded or contaminated (p. 619). Terri describes a contaminated saliva control that cleared when she repeated the amplification, and Carly says contamination can persist with no identifiable cause (p. 619). In the paper's description, conclusions often took repeated interpretation and discussion between analyst and reviewer, sometimes with others brought in (p. 619), and Terri remarks that writing a report could take the wider laboratory (p. 619). What goes out is a profile released after technical and administrative review (pp. 617–618) and a report that pairs a contributor conclusion with a population-frequency figure (p. 618). And the method became established over roughly twenty-five years, after technical advances, court challenges and favorable National Academy assessments in the 1990s (p. 617, which the paper draws from cited sources). The wager from this side: the forensic biology unit is not the fixed point the other three are measured from but one more unit whose work is judgment talked through with a reviewer, and whose occupation was itself under court challenge and Academy assessment first. The firearms review in the passage on p. 622, two examiners debating how much agreement is enough, is the nearest printed counterpart to the passage on p. 619. Review of an analyst's work by someone else is printed for every unit (pp. 617–618 with p. 619, p. 622, pp. 625–626, pp. 629–630); what is printed for forensic biology alone is the population-frequency figure (p. 618). If so, what each neighbor is compared with (the paper's claim at p. 617, p. 634) and found compatible or incompatible with (the paper's claim at p. 606, p. 608, p. 617, p. 620, p. 625, pp. 627–628, p. 632, pp. 633–637; Table 2, Technique — firearms, p. 633; Table 2, Technique — toxicology, p. 633; Table 2, Technique — controlled substances (narcotics), p. 633, author's account) is what leaves the DNA unit, and the judgment that the paper's table sets against the objectivity associated with DNA (Table 2, Values — firearms, p. 633, author's account) is present on the DNA side as well (p. 619). This agrees with the paper on the substance of the paper's claim (pp. 618–619), untidy work and outputs that look objective, and uses the same passages. It differs in where it puts the unit: among the cases, with a history of being evaluated, and not above them. Whether the review steps and the figure are what that earlier evaluation left behind is not printed, and the reading does not assert it.

'Change to practice' covers two things. X is a change that leaves in place the way the result is reached and adds to what is recorded, shown or reported with it. Y is a change that replaces the person's own looking and judging as the way the identification is reached. On the X side: firearms examiners say knowing a mark on sight is no longer acceptable and images must back the call (p. 622); they keep note packets with images of each set of striae to support judgment on the stand (p. 621); a second examiner signs each page (p. 622); toxicology adds an uncertainty range with the same instrument and method (p. 627, p. 628); narcotics analysts talk over buying microscope cameras (p. 632). On the Y side: counting striae is not regularly used (p. 623), numbers are declined (p. 624), and a move to GC/MS is feared or refused (p. 631, p. 632). Read this way the three units look alike: each has taken on or entertained an X change, none is printed taking on a Y change, and toxicology is not printed as being asked for one. The contrast between embracing and resisting would then lie partly in which kind of change each unit was presented with. This sits close to the paper's values account for the Y passages; it departs from the paper on firearms, where an X change is printed as already made.

Read the direction the other way: what the paper calls a unit's values is partly a record of who came, who stayed and who left. Taylor took the toxicology job as the one that was open, did that work, wanted out, and persuaded management to train her elsewhere (p. 630); several narcotics analysts had worked in toxicology and been eager to move (p. 630). Neha says a 'normal person' sometimes arrives in toxicology and irritates the rest (p. 626). Billie ties her liking for crystal tests to being a chemist and to not wanting to repeat one task, and says other people would prefer the instrument (p. 632). Analysts are hired into a specific unit (p. 613). On this reading the same technique did not produce the same values in everyone who performed it, and the narcotics unit's dislike of standardised work would be something its members brought with them out of toxicology. The units' different responses would then track who is in them.

What the paper calls occupational values are, at this site, partly the residue of sorting inside one lab. Analysts with the same degrees are placed where there is an opening, can be reassigned by the director, and can lobby to be retrained; several of those now in narcotics had left toxicology because they could not stand its routine. Their recoil from instrument-first drug testing, and the toxicologists' ease with error figures, would then describe who ended up at which bench as much as what each kind of work teaches. A forced change of method would be met with transfer requests as well as resistance, a response the paper's embrace-or-resist pair leaves out. Analysts arrive with the same kinds of degree and are hired into a particular unit after tests and a panel interview (p. 613). Placement is the employer's decision about similar recruits. All are [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 619] are treated as interchangeable; the director plans to swap two analysts between narcotics and firearms and tells staff that each of them ought to be deployable anywhere in the lab (pp. 619–620). The units appear as postings. Several narcotics analysts had worked in toxicology and wanted out; one took the toxicology job because it was the opening, found it slow to leave, and persuaded management to train them elsewhere; the unit calls toxicology's work mind-numbing (p. 630). Entry by vacancy and exit by preference is sorting, and the contrast the paper reads as occupational values is voiced by people who left. A toxicologist remarks that an occasional 'normal person' in the unit annoys the rest (p. 626). Fit between person and unit varies and is policed, as selection would predict. An analyst frames her liking for crystal tests as personal: other people would prefer the instrument and she is not one of them (p. 632). Preference is attached to persons. Interviews covered career histories (p. 614). The material that would test the sorting account was gathered. The paper leaves open how neighboring occupations should be bounded (p. 636). This is its own invitation to ask whether these are occupations or postings.

The construct does two jobs. In X passages the speaker or the quoted text itself holds other work up against DNA: the NAS excerpt sets toolmark-type tests beside [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 620] (p. 620); an examiner at the statewide meeting says they cannot be like DNA (p. 624); a narcotics analyst voices the demand as one made of firearms (p. 624); Tom and Pete talk about statistics and numbers when the author asks what being like DNA means (p. 624). In Y passages a demand is reported and the speaker names another source for it: Jason names ISO and NIST documents and scientific fields in general and denies that NAS spurred it (p. 627); Jodi names NAS 'and other attacks', East Coast practice and the lack of an output others can review (p. 631); Robin names a Daubert hearing on crystal testing (p. 632); Taylor and Billie name East Coast instrument routine (p. 632). In the Y passages the tie to DNA is supplied by the author's characterisation (p. 627, p. 628, p. 632). Read this way, the firearms unit met a comparison with DNA, while toxicology and narcotics met demands for a stated measurement uncertainty or a reviewable output that no printed toxicologist or narcotics analyst attributes to DNA in respect of their own work. The three-way difference in response would then be partly a difference in what was asked and by whom, not three answers to one question.

Read this way, values did not sort the DNA comparison into welcome or threat in advance; they were the language in which a response settled by exposure and feasibility was narrated afterward. Toxicologists changed because a court challenge loomed and a plan existed, then presented accuracy as what they had always prized. Narcotics analysts could not shift to instrumentation with two machines and a statutory turnaround clock; the praise of craft followed. Firearms examiners unchallenged at home called holism a virtue, while those who had faced admissibility hearings elsewhere urged examining bias. Values are the sediment of what a group has had to do, not a sieve. Values are said to be rooted in the work itself, with toxicologists prizing accuracy because they have seen what lapses in technique produce (p. 637). The author's own account derives values from practice, which licenses reading them as consequences of what a group has done rather than the gate on what it will do. Locally unchallenged MCCL examiners stood pat while [8 words of Bechky (2020), p. 635] admissibility hearings seemed moved to change, and the paper adds that the pathway created the occasion for meaning-making (pp. 635–636). With values held constant, exposure did the sorting, and the articulation of values belongs to the meaning-making that followed. Toxicologists already held an ISO plan for uncertainty of measurement, enacted it at once when the challenge appeared, and Jason then told the criminal justice community the lab had been doing this all along (pp. 627–628). The decision was made by the court date and the accreditation calendar; the fit with error-free values was composed afterwards for an audience. Jodi and Robin explain the trouble with GC/MS as longer runs, two instruments and a caseload the lab could not keep up with, before the complaints about boredom and lost craft (pp. 631–632). The infeasibility is spelled out in capacity and time, and the values language is layered over that constraint. An examiner who had faced defense challenges argued the critics were working from examiners' own testimony and called the attacks a useful motivator, while others called for scrutiny of bias (pp. 623–624). Examiners sharing the same craft advocated change once they had been on the stand; the direction of response tracked exposure, not a difference in values.

The contrast between toxicology and narcotics could partly result from people sorting themselves into work they already preferred. Employees who disliked repetitive processing sought transfers, leaving units increasingly populated by people who valued their characteristic tasks. Management's hiring and transfer arrangements would help produce the apparently distinct occupational cultures. Responses to proposed changes would then reflect accumulated staffing choices as well as values learned through doing the work. Criminalists entered with similar educational backgrounds but were hired into particular units (p. 613). This places the starting distinction inside an organizational assignment process rather than demonstrating that entrants already belonged to wholly separate professional populations. The author describes criminalists as potentially interchangeable across units and introduces a director's plan to exchange narcotics and firearms staff (p. 619). This supplies an organizational route through which unit membership could change. Several narcotics analysts had previously worked in toxicology and wanted to leave (p. 630). One explained taking the available toxicology position and later persuading management to arrange training elsewhere because the balance of paperwork and benchwork was unsatisfying. This is direct evidence of preference influencing movement between units. Toxicologists described colleagues who did not share their organizational habits as irritating exceptions (p. 626). This shows that fit within a unit was noticed and policed, which could reinforce selection, although the passage does not show anyone leaving because of it.

The toxicology episode could be read as the accelerated completion of an existing accreditation project. The laboratory already possessed the data, procedures, and plan needed to report measurement uncertainty; an impending courtroom challenge supplied a deadline. DNA supplied a persuasive comparison, but might not have determined the reform's content or eventual adoption. On this reading, the central change was when an established obligation became urgent, rather than which neighboring technology became exemplary. A defense attorney's successful challenges elsewhere and an anticipated local challenge brought measurement uncertainty to immediate attention, although the NAS report had not criticized toxicological analysis (p. 625). This locates the trigger in an organized litigation strategy rather than a newly identified technical defect. Before the NAS report appeared, MCCL was preparing for ISO accreditation requirements and toxicology had a three-year uncertainty-estimation plan (p. 627). The threatened testimony prompted immediate implementation. This supplies the chronology needed to read the event as acceleration of a prior commitment. At an outreach session, a toxicologist disputed the claim that laboratories had only begun addressing uncertainty because of the NAS report and invoked other scientific standards (p. 627). His account gives the existing program an explicitly different origin, although it is also a public defense of the laboratory. The toxicologist described using the same instrument and method for five years and combining previously collected quality-control information with assessments of procedural uncertainty (p. 628). This supports continuity in analysis beneath the new reporting practice.

The central change could be a redistribution of the ability to check an expert's conclusion. Durable images, instrument records, and explicit uncertainty calculations allow people who were absent from the original analysis to revisit parts of it. DNA's authority would then rest partly on making judgments available for later inspection, and the other units' disputes would concern how much of their work could be reopened by reviewers and legal audiences. This reading makes control over subsequent scrutiny the organizing issue, extending beyond whether an occupation regards a technique as scientifically appropriate. Legal parties could inspect DNA documentation, while the observed production of a DNA report involved anomalies, interpretation, and collective judgment (p. 619). This combination suggests that inspectable records can carry authority even when the underlying work remains dependent on expert judgment. Firearms examiners assembled detailed images to support their conclusions in testimony, and an examiner invoked outsiders' previous reviews of his work (p. 621). This links documentary practice to the capacity to withstand later inspection. Firearms examiners described a historical shift toward image-backed documentation and worked together to select persuasive views of a comparison (p. 622). The record offered for inspection was itself actively constructed, making the distribution of checking rights inseparable from decisions about what would be visible. A narcotics analyst identified the absence of a lasting, independently checkable output from crystal testing as a reason the method might lose acceptance (p. 631). This isolates later reviewability as a vulnerability even though the analyst considered the identification scientifically sound. The proposed remedies included another analyst's visual review and cameras on microscopes (p. 632). These proposals would change who could inspect the result and when, without necessarily replacing the underlying chemistry.

One condition accounts for all three outcomes: whether an analyst in this lab expected to be personally challenged in the local court. Toxicology had such a date and changed. Firearms and narcotics did not and stayed as they were. Occupational values then add nothing to the explanation. They describe how each unit talked about a decision that local exposure had already made. Because the study has one lab, each occupation appears under only one exposure condition, so the paper cannot tell values from exposure. A named local case with an out-of-state expert was about to challenge toxicology results (p. 625). This is the only unit with a local court date. Firearms [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 624] the county's jurisdiction, and the examiners did not change in response to pressure from elsewhere (p. 624). The paper notes that [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 635] been through admissibility hearings seemed motivated to change practice (p. 635). These are members of the same occupation, with different exposure and a different stance. An examiner from outside who had faced such questioning urges colleagues to treat the critics as a spur to do better (pp. 623–624). This again links exposure to willingness. A narcotics analyst attended a workshop on an admissibility hearing that challenged crystal testing (p. 632). Narcotics, like firearms, had a court challenge somewhere else and none at home. The paper's own summary says narcotics had [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 632] change and therefore kept its practices (p. 632). Fieldwork was three to six months per unit within eighteen months that began the month the report came out, so units were also seen at different distances from the report's release (p. 614).

The units could share a practical rule: revise established work when a credible local challenge makes continuing costly, and otherwise defend it. The observed contrast between adoption and resistance would then reflect different positions in a sequence of exposure to consequences, more than enduring differences in willingness to change. Occupational values would supply the language and acceptable form of adjustment, while the likelihood of losing the ability to testify would determine whether adjustment happened. This wager gives local consequences greater explanatory weight than the paper's joint account of pathways, techniques, and values. MCCL firearms examiners had not faced challenges in their own jurisdiction, whereas a presenter who had encountered questioning elsewhere treated criticism as a reason to improve practice (p. 624). Variation inside firearms examination makes actual exposure a candidate explanation for divergent responses within an ostensibly shared occupational culture. Toxicologists moved from a multi-year plan to immediate implementation when an upcoming local case threatened their testimony (p. 627). This is a concrete example of perceived consequences changing the timing of action. The narcotics debate had not yet imposed an immediate requirement, and analysts continued their preferred practices (p. 632). Their observed resistance could therefore be a position maintained while the disputed rule remained unsettled. Firearms examiners described having previously moved from personal assurances toward systematic visual documentation (p. 622). Their own history demonstrates some capacity to accommodate external expectations while retaining expert judgment.

Read the ending as provisional at its near edge as well as its far one. The paper closes with three units inside the comparison's reach and the outer boundary unknown (p. 636, author's account). In print the three do not sit inside it in the same way. Firearms: the NAS report says techniques such as toolmark comparison had not received stringent testing, lacked known error rates and had produced some erroneous results when compared with DNA evidence (p. 620); a SWG-GUN board member says attempts to exclude firearms evidence were becoming more common (p. 621); an examiner at the statewide meeting says firearms work could not simply be made equivalent to DNA analysis (p. 624). Narcotics: an analyst describes the demand on non-DNA specialties as pressure to become more like DNA analysis (p. 617), and Jodi fears crystal testing could be phased out because it leaves no persistent instrument output for later review (p. 631); the participant link to DNA on this side is the passage on p. 617 alone, and it is stated for non-DNA specialties in general. Toxicology: the report did not criticize toxicology directly (p. 625); the uncertainty plan predates the report (p. 627); the requirements named are ISO, NIST, state law and ASCLD (p. 627, pp. 627–628); the courtroom attack is on reports that omit uncertainty estimates (p. 625); and Jason rejects the idea that the laboratory had only begun the work because of the report (pp. 627–628). No toxicology passage has a toxicologist, or the attorney, naming DNA. That toxicologists encountered the DNA comparison through that case is the author's account (p. 627; Table 2, Institutional pathways of spillover — toxicology, p. 633; p. 634). The wager: the edge that the paper's open question (p. 636) looks for beyond the three may run between them, with toxicology, the one unit recorded as changing its practice (Table 2, Response of group at MCCL — toxicology, p. 633, author's account), on the far side. If so, the sorter ventured in the paper's claim (p. 634, p. 636) does not find the edge, because the three units share a laboratory, a director who says all are criminalists who should be capable of working in any unit (pp. 619–620), and, on the paper's account, their audiences (p. 636). The ending would also change shape: the comparison reached two units and, on the paper's own record, changed local practice in neither (Table 2, Response of group at MCCL — firearms, p. 633; Table 2, Response of group at MCCL — controlled substances (narcotics), p. 633, author's account), while the unit that changed did so under requirements and a courtroom strategy whose tie to DNA is printed only in the author's voice. The far edge is no better fixed. The only named forensic occupation in print beyond the three and DNA is the trace examiners, whose flyer said trace work had been pushed behind DNA work and whose printed concern is attention and resources (p. 619); no passage has their methods evaluated against DNA's.

Narcotics analysts' resistance could be read as the defense of a workable service under binding equipment and turnaround constraints. Their ability to perform GC/MS did not establish that their unit could process its whole workload that way. On this reading, the apparent mismatch between technical compatibility and refusal to change is largely a mismatch between knowing a method and having the capacity to use it at scale. Craft values make the defense compelling to analysts, but insufficient capacity would be enough to sustain it. Local charging requirements imposed rapid turnaround, and the unit's common methamphetamine cases could often be confirmed with crystal tests in roughly ten to fifteen minutes (p. 629). Analysts already used GC/MS for unfamiliar substances or cases that crystal testing could not resolve. This presents the existing mixture of methods as a practical allocation of limited processing time. Analysts objected to delays introduced by a new reporting system and discussed saving individual minutes in data entry (p. 631). This shows that sensitivity to throughput extended beyond a dispute over scientific identity or instrumentation. An analyst said that two instruments and lengthy runs could not accommodate the caseload (p. 632). The group also considered duplicate crystal tests and microscope cameras, comparing their time and purchase costs. These passages supply concrete bottlenecks and show attention to alternative ways of meeting review demands.

The comparison with DNA could be read as a struggle over making expert work inspectable after the analyst has finished. DNA's authority rests partly on durable records that let evidence travel to reviewers and courts, while substantial judgment remains inside its production. The proposed reforms would therefore redistribute the ability to question an analysis, not simply replace subjectivity with objectivity. Firearms examiners may already have accommodated part of this demand through imaging, even while resisting the particular demand for statistical matching. Legal parties could inspect DNA records, yet analysts described contamination, imperfect graphs, and conclusions reached through extensive collective interpretation (p. 619). This separates the availability of a reviewable record from the absence of expert discretion. Firearms examiners assembled detailed images and notes to sustain testimony and emphasized that outsiders had inspected their work (p. 621). This shows that documentary accessibility was already part of their defense of expert judgment. Examiners described an earlier shift toward mandatory documentation, and the observed review involved negotiating both an identification and the images that would substantiate it (p. 622). This makes their apparent resistance compatible with prior adaptation in the form of evidence they produced. A narcotics analyst identified the inability of others to revisit a crystal observation as a reason the method might be prohibited (p. 631). The threatened deficiency concerns access to the evidentiary trace, even though she regarded the test as reliable. The proposed remedies included another analyst examining crystals or cameras preserving their appearance (p. 632). These would change who could inspect the result without necessarily requiring abandonment of crystal chemistry, helping isolate reviewability as a distinct demand.

Toxicology's change was an accreditation step brought forward, not a response to DNA profiling. Its content, an uncertainty figure built largely from quality-control data the unit already held, was set by a plan the unit had before it heard of the challenge, part of ISO work begun before the report appeared. A DUI defense tactic already succeeding in other states decided the timing. DNA enters only through the paper's own statements about what the attorney would argue. If so, the one case of embraced change shows codified lab standards and DUI litigation at work, and says little about whether a neighbor's technology moves anyone. The report hardly mentions toxicology and does not fault it, and the line of attack (lab reports that leave out an uncertainty estimate) was already winning DUI cases elsewhere and being taught to other attorneys (p. 625). The challenge has a history of its own in DUI litigation, and the tactic as described makes no reference to DNA. Before the report came out the lab was aligning itself with ISO 17025 (printed as 17205 in a quotation lower on the page) on its accreditor's recommendation, and the unit held a three-year plan for estimating uncertainty when it first heard of the challenge (p. 627). The content of the change is fixed ahead of the trigger. At an outreach session an analyst denies that labs are scrambling because of the report, says the unit was 'already doing it', and cites general measurement documents (p. 627). The unit's own public account plays down the report and makes no comparison with DNA. The instrument has been the same for five years and the method is unchanged; the uncertainty figure is assembled from quality-control data already on file plus a step-by-step assessment of the procedure, and what is new is a range and a confidence level on the report (p. 628). The change has the size and shape of a planned compliance step. The lab directors' association (the lab's accreditor, p. 627) urged managers to ready their staff for courtroom questions about the report (p. 616). The accreditor, not the example of the DNA unit, is the channel into the lab. The discussion grants that accreditation-driven changes already under way made the response easier (p. 635). What the paper treats as an enabling condition is, in this reading, the cause.

The toxicology case is not a spillover from DNA profiling. It is an accreditation project that was already under way and was brought forward by one court date. Read this way, the toxicologists changed their reports because ISO-based accreditation required uncertainty estimates and a defence attorney was about to ask for them. The comparison with DNA is something the analyst attaches to the episode, not something the toxicologists were responding to. The paper would then have two cases of DNA comparison (firearms, narcotics) and one case of ordinary standards compliance. The national report hardly mentions toxicology and does not criticise it, so the comparison with DNA has no direct textual route to this unit (p. 625). The trigger is a defence attorney who had won DUI cases elsewhere on missing uncertainty estimates, and a specific local case planning the same challenge (p. 625). The complaint is about measurement uncertainty, not about DNA. Before the report appeared, the lab was already revising protocols to an ISO standard that required a plan for estimating measurement uncertainty (p. 627). The change predates the supposed cause. A toxicologist tells an outreach audience that it is untrue that labs added uncertainty because of the report, and that the lab was already doing it (p. 627). The members' own account denies the spillover. The estimate is built from five years of quality-control data the lab had already collected with an unchanged method, which shows continuity of practice and no new comparison (p. 628). The discussion itself concedes that changes already being made for accreditation made the response easier (p. 635).

The narcotics dispute could be retold as competition within an occupation over whose established equipment and methods would become compulsory for everyone. DNA's prestige would serve as an argument available to a regional coalition seeking to make its own practice the national rule. The consequential difference would be access to standard-setting authority, with occupational values shaping what each side defended. This would give power a more central role than the paper's explanation allows, without assuming that the proposed standards lacked scientific merit. The paper describes an existing regional division between instrument-based analysis and crystal testing and says that the community accepted both methods as scientifically valid (p. 628). Renewed comparison with DNA could therefore change the relative standing of already legitimate alternatives rather than introduce an entirely new technical problem. MCCL analysts feared that Eastern practitioners, whom they believed disproportionately represented on the scientific working group's board, could prohibit crystal testing (p. 631). This connects their anxiety to perceived control of rule-making, although it does not verify the board's composition or intentions. The working group's existing requirement for two different crystal tests already organized MCCL's practice (p. 630). This establishes that its standards could reach the bench, making a prospective prohibition more consequential than a difference in professional opinion alone. MCCL's limited instrument capacity meant that adopting the preferred alternative would impose substantial local costs (p. 632). This identifies what the unit could lose if another region's existing arrangements became the general requirement.

The narcotics unit kept crystal tests because, on a legal clock and with two instruments, it could not clear its cases any other way; that is the reason an analyst gave when describing a hearing that contested the method. On this reading the unit was neither sheltered inside a professional debate nor chiefly defending a craft. It was holding a position set by statute and equipment while pricing the cheapest way to leave a reviewable record. Its veteran analyst expected the move to instruments, and given the capacity most of the unit would make it. The law requires quick turnaround because charges depend on which drug and how much; the commonest drug is confirmed by crystals in 10–15 minutes, and GC/MS is already used for samples crystals cannot settle (p. 629). This sets the clock and shows the instrument in use, without recorded objection, where it is needed. A veteran analyst names the method's weakness (nothing others can check later), expects the unit will probably have to move to GC/MS, and objects that it takes longer (p. 631). Compliance is anticipated, with time as the stated cost. Describing a workshop on a Daubert hearing against crystal testing, an analyst says the county could not keep up without crystals, having two instruments and long runs (p. 632). Capacity is the reason given, in a court context. A second viewer would double analysis time, and microscope cameras, though costly, would be far cheaper than more instruments (p. 632). Analysts are weighing fixes by time and money and already considering change. Analysts time themselves and press for fixes to a new records system that slowed their cases (p. 631). Speed is a standing concern, one the paper lists among the unit's values (p. 630), though Table 2 (p. 633) names only autonomy and variety as what the comparison offends. Table 2 records no court pathway for narcotics, and p. 635 says the unit met no court challenges of any kind; challenges to firearms evidence, likewise in other jurisdictions and relayed at a professional meeting (p. 621), are coded yes (p. 633). This is the coding the passage unsettles.

Read the narcotics outcome as where things stood when fieldwork ended in August 2010 (p. 612), not as an ending. Jodi expects the crystal test to be phased out and GC/MS to take its place (p. 631). The working group is still debating a second analyst's check (p. 632). The unit is weighing cameras against instruments on cost (p. 632). Robin has attended a workshop on a recent Daubert hearing against crystal testing (p. 632). What is printed as resistance is talk at benches and in meetings (p. 615) about preferences, time and cost; no instruction to change is printed, and no refusal of one. The objections that carry quantities are about capacity: two instruments and long runs (p. 632), and a legal requirement of short turnaround (p. 629). If the working group ruled against the crystal test, the printed material would support reading the unit's holding on as a matter of nothing yet being required and of capacity, with values shaping how the prospect was talked about. Robin's hearing also gives narcotics a court challenge heard about at a professional event, the same shape as the one firearms examiners heard about at theirs (p. 621), where the author records none for narcotics (p. 635; p. 633).

Attribute the difference to what the paper treats as a facilitator. Before the NAS report the lab was already conforming to ISO 17025, and toxicology had a three-year plan to estimate uncertainty of measurement (p. 627). Its protocol already required a log tracing instruments, reagents and standards, and state law already required a confidence interval (p. 627). It had quality-control data from more than five years on an unchanged method (p. 628). On hearing of the challenge the unit brought the plan forward (p. 627). Jason tells a criminal-justice audience that labs were not scrambling on account of NAS and that the work was already being done (p. 627). On this reading the two units differ in whether the answer to the challenge was already scheduled by the accreditor; the nearness of the court case accounts for the date, not for the change. No comparable scheduled item is printed for the firearms unit. The reading agrees with the paper that ASCLD's requirements mattered (p. 633, p. 635) and departs from it only in putting them first.

The units did not embrace or resist being like DNA as a whole. Each took up the one feature of DNA evidence it could reach and declined the rest. The feature that matters across all three is a record that someone else can inspect afterwards. Firearms had already moved to it, with images of every comparison and a second examiner signing each page, while refusing numbers. Narcotics was exposed because the crystal test leaves nothing to inspect, and its talk of cameras and second viewers is the start of the same move. On this reading the firearms unit is a case of change the paper does not count, and the embrace/resist outcome column hides a shared shift toward reviewable documentation. DNA's standing is tied to graphs, tables and raw data that legal parties can review (pp. 618–619). This identifies the reviewable record as the feature being compared. A visible record of matching marks is described as important because it backs the examiner on the stand (p. 621). One examiner says outsiders have reviewed his packets without challenge. Examiners say the old appeal to recognition by eye is no longer acceptable and that images are now required (p. 622). This is a reported change in practice in the direction of DNA-style documentation. A second examiner looks at every set of marks and signs every page, and the two discuss lighting and angle to make the image more convincing (p. 622). The work is aimed at an outside reader. The same examiners decline the counting method (p. 623). The refusal is specific to quantification, not to documentation. A narcotics analyst locates the crystal test's weakness in the fact that it produces no output others can check later (p. 631). The working group debates a second viewer and the unit discusses microscope cameras (p. 632). Narcotics is considering the documentation route firearms already took. The unit already runs a second, different crystal test on each sample to meet working-group guidelines, so it does adjust practice to outside standards (p. 630).

The responses are moves to protect or improve each unit's standing and its members' irreplaceability inside a lab whose director treats all analysts as interchangeable. Narcotics and firearms defend long craft training because it makes them hard to swap and keeps them above routine instrument work. Toxicology, which other units look down on as button-pressing, takes up uncertainty reporting because it raises the unit's standing. This reverses the paper's claim that status and power mattered much less [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 637]. The envy the paper names is first described as envy of the DNA unit's equipment, money and staff, and trace examiners form a new association over lost attention (p. 619). The comparison is experienced as a matter of standing and resources. The director, planning to swap analysts between narcotics and firearms, tells staff they should all [7 words of Bechky (2020), p. 620] (pp. 619–620). Interchangeability is an active managerial position. Firearms examiners train for two years and DNA analysts for nine months before casework (p. 620). Long training is the barrier against being swapped. Narcotics analysts describe toxicology work as mind-numbing and several had left that unit (p. 630). This shows a ranking among units by the kind of work done. An analyst says anyone off the street could run the instrument method, whereas crystal testing needs validation and training (p. 632). The objection is about who could replace them. A firearms examiner resents colleagues elsewhere who think counting makes them more objective than he is (p. 623). This is a contest over standing within the occupation. Toxicologists are visibly proud when presenting their new error reporting to the criminal justice community (p. 628). The table records toxicology's value response with a remark that the county is ahead of the rest of the state on error measurement, which is a claim to rank (p. 633).

The toxicology episode could be read as an existing accreditation reform brought forward by litigation. On this reading, the new reporting practice had already acquired its rationale, materials, and organizational commitment before the comparison with DNA became urgent. DNA supplied a persuasive courtroom reference for accelerating that project. The wager is that the reform's content and eventual adoption can be explained without making technological spillover their initiating cause; the spillover primarily changed the timetable. Before the NAS report appeared, the laboratory was preparing for ISO accreditation, and toxicology already had a three-year plan to estimate measurement uncertainty (p. 627). Analysts implemented that plan immediately when they learned of the anticipated courtroom challenge. This supplies a sequence in which the project precedes the pressure used to explain its implementation. In an outreach presentation, a toxicologist disputed the suggestion that the NAS report had initiated the uncertainty work, cited standards from several scientific settings, and described historical data collected under an earlier protocol (p. 627). This provides an actor's explicit alternative account of the reform's origin, although the public presentation could also be self-protective. The presentation described an unchanged instrument and method, with existing quality-control information combined into a new uncertainty calculation (p. 628). This locates the change in the statistical treatment and reporting of established work rather than in the introduction of a new analytic process.

The four identification types are stations on a membership career, not separate products of practices succeeding or failing. Entry brings a burst of enthusiasm. The first year brings a crisis in which many leave, indifferent or angry. Survivors either deepen or settle into a long, low-cost stall. The branching diagram is then a cross-section of people caught at different points on one time course, and 'success' and 'failure' of practices name where someone currently stands. All former distributors interviewed had left within a year, inactive ones had been members for at least a year and a half, and actives ranged up to two decades (p. 461). Exit clusters early and inactivity appears only after the first year. A distributor singles out the first few months as the hardest (p. 474). There is a recognised early trial. A former distributor describes initial excitement followed by fading interest (p. 477). This is a sequence within one person, which the paper files as a type. Among the successful, dreams shift over time from lifestyle to family to saving the country (p. 468). Positive identification itself has stages. Footnote 13 notes that members who stop selling are kept in the fold for a long time before being dropped (p. 473). The organisation treats inactivity as a phase. Ambivalent members cycle between bursts of activity and long pauses (p. 481). Their state is described as movement. The paper states that distributors moved between identification states in several directions but does not discuss this in detail (p. 485). The trajectories exist in the data and are not printed.

The pair is the analyst's, a weaker footing than one the paper drew. As printed, each passage has a before and an after, and in each the before runs against the state the episode is filed under. The distributor in the passage on p. 476 had ignored her upline's advice in that recruiting attempt; the conclusion that the upline and the recordings had foreseen her friends' reaction came after. The distributor in the passage on p. 480 had Amway merchandise on display at work; the denial came after a coworker tied Amway to Nazis. The paper's account gives the first a reliance on upline sources (p. 475, the author's account) and the second a standing embarrassment (the author's characterisation on p. 480). The passages print people being moved by an event, the direction the paper's claim (p. 484) leaves open: the episode first, the stance after. The two responses are also not the same kind of thing. The passage on p. 480 prints what a distributor did at once, on the remark. The passage on p. 476 prints what a distributor concluded afterwards and told the researcher. Two other passages filed with the passage on p. 476 are of the second kind: a confrontation retold in celebration at a dinner (p. 475), and friends' avoidance retold as a lesson about those friends (p. 475). In the two places where the paper prints the moment of facing an outsider's doubt about Amway, it prints giving way: the denial in the passage on p. 480, and the researcher's enthusiasm weakening among skeptical colleagues, whom he then avoided (p. 481). The wager is that the pair shows two moments of one sequence and not two kinds of member. In front of the outsider the member gives ground; afterwards, away from the outsider, the organization's account turns the same blow into a point in its favor. What the paper files as a mixed state would be the first moment, and what it files as reliance on upline sources the second. The second moment is close to what the paper itself claims (pp. 473–475, p. 487); the difference is that the paper sorts members and this reading sorts moments.

The paper's hedge makes leaving the end that the practices come to when they fail on a member. Read as provisional, the departures in print are not that end; they come before the practices have run. Every former distributor interviewed had [6 words of Pratt (2000), p. 461] (p. 461). Their accounts are of an early appeal that faded (p. 477), of something tried that did not suit (p. 478), of a regular job that became satisfying (pp. 477–478), of buying in to get out of an embarrassing situation at a presentation (p. 479). The printed figures agree that staying active is not the usual course: a secondary source puts yearly leaving between about two-fifths and nearly all of the membership (p. 477), and Amway's own publication counts fewer than half of recorded distributors as active (p. 463). The practices, meanwhile, are printed as working by repetition and over time: an achieved dream is to be replaced by a larger one (p. 468), no achievement is to be taken as a final peak (p. 468), successful distributors' aspirations shifted over time (p. 468), and by the author's account encapsulation grew as members spent more time with other distributors (p. 473). On this reading the order in the paper's claim (p. 477) turns over. The leavers did not go because identification failed to take; they went early, before the repeated work the paper describes had been done on them, and identification was not secured because they had gone. Leaving in the first year is then one thing and the failure of the practices another, and the leavers in print speak only to the first. Where the practices fail would show in people who left after long, active membership. The paper comes near such people twice and prints no account from either: distributors who reached high sales levels before quitting (p. 463), whose length of membership is not given, and distributors who moved away from positive identification (p. 485), of whom it is not said whether any left.

Start the episode at the recruitment meeting and the second disidentified informant's story is complete before the paper's episode opens. He describes how his sponsor got him in: a sales talk, people around him saying positive things, a slide show, being there in someone else's car, strong social pressure, and paying about $120 as the easiest way out; he says he felt humiliated and likens it to a torture session (p. 479). In that passage the unfavourable reading of the sponsor is already in place at the moment of joining, and joining is described as an exit from the room, not as the pursuit of anything wanted. Nothing printed for him shows a dream, an upline relationship that then went wrong, or a confidant. The recruitment meeting is also not empty of the practices the paper studies: an Emerald distributor addresses a group of prospects at a meeting that is also a dream-building session (p. 466), and the first disidentified informant locates what attracted him at the outset, in the look of his recruiter's home (p. 478). On this reading recruitment is where an identification in opposition can be set, and 'successfully recruited' covers both a prospect who was drawn in (p. 478) and one who paid to get out (p. 479).

Read for what distributors did rather than what they believed, the paper supports a plainer account of positive identification: it is the residue of freely chosen, costly, public action. Dream building and positive programming produce it together because each is an occasion for enactment—trying on suits before one's upline, paying for tapes and functions, approaching relatives first and then withdrawing from them. Freely taken acts bind the actor, and cognition reorganizes to justify them. Identification thus tracks the dose of enactment, is indifferent to financial return, and fails where the committing act was coerced. The meaning void comes afterward, as the committed person's story of why she committed. Removes payoff as the explanation: identification bore no relation to financial success, nobody could state a net profit, and average gross income was trivial — what one expects if attachment grows from money and effort already spent rather than from returns (p. 463). Provides the paper's own aside that as distributors spent more time pursuing dreams, more of their lives became bound up with the distributor identity, which the paper itself labels behavioral commitment; the reading moves this aside to the center of the account (p. 469). States the process in the paper's own terms — enacting positive programming involves choice, freely chosen behavior is highly committing, and behaving as a distributor leads to thinking of oneself as one — and documents the bridge-burning of approaching relatives first and then withdrawing from them, acts hard to reverse that foreclose exits (p. 474). Anchors the outcome and its wording: positive identification appeared when both practices succeeded, is described as continuously enacted and reenacted, and best characterized active distributors; the reading takes the word enacted literally (p. 476). Marks the boundary condition: the former distributor who disidentified recalls being sold under intense social pressure and paying as the easiest way out of an awkward room, then feeling humiliated — an act without volition, which on this reading cannot bind and instead breeds resentment (p. 479).

Read the other way round, not distributing comes first and the intact non-member ties are its result. No printed passage from an ambivalent distributor reports being advised against Amway by a non-member. The one informant who addresses the point says nobody tells him he cannot or should not do it, that everybody says it works, and that the not-starting is down to him (p. 480). What the other passages print is abstention: one inactive distributor does not bring lists, does not sponsor and does not use the products consistently (p. 480); another now calls only people he does not see much of (p. 480). On the author's own account, approaching family and friends is how a distributor finds out which relationships are negative (author's characterisation on p. 474; an active distributor describes the first months of approaching them as the hardest, p. 474). A distributor who does not approach never runs that test, so nothing has happened that would lead to those ties being dropped. On this reading the ambivalence printed on p. 480 is between wanting to start and not starting, not between two sets of advisers, and the kept ties are a trace of the inactivity rather than its cause.

This group speaks in one passage, so the retelling is short. Asked for their net profit, current and former distributors did two things: they did not produce a clear figure, and they disagreed among themselves about which product margins and which training expenses belong in the sum (p. 463). The paper takes this as a limit on what could be measured and goes on to conclude that money did not sort people (the paper's claim at p. 463). Told from the distributors' side it is a report about them. Among the people doing this work, what the business earns is not a settled number; it depends on what one is prepared to call a cost. The cost in dispute is not a small one. Distributors paid for their training (p. 459), and the training is printed as a system of books, recordings, meetings, rallies and seminars (p. 459); books and tapes are also among the media through which members met model dreams (pp. 465–466). Whoever leaves those expenses out has a business that nets more than whoever puts them in. The wager is that the disagreement in the passage on p. 463 ran between those who stood with [6 words of Pratt (2000), p. 462], and that counting the training as a cost of the business, or not counting it, is itself a way of standing toward the organization. If that is so, financial result cannot be laid beside identification as a separate measure, as the passage on p. 463 lays it, since a distributor's own figure already holds an answer to what the training is. This does not dispute that money failed to sort people; it disputes that money was a separate thing to sort them by. The passage does not say along what line the disagreement ran, and it leaves 'could not' and 'would not' unseparated.

The paper sets the two men side by side as failed support and durable support. The passages print something narrower: what each upline did with a member the pair holds to have been less than fully active. In the passage on p. 479 what the upline offered came through the program: it relied mainly on more meetings. In the passage on p. 480 what the sponsor offered stood apart from the program: the support went on while he repeatedly failed to attend functions, prepare lists, recruit or use the products consistently, and the sponsor used a kinship term for him. Elsewhere what uplines give is printed as running through the work. The researcher's upline tolerated his interviewing so long as he kept selling and trying to recruit (p. 460), and one distributor wanted the Pearl level partly so that he could join golf trips with upline members he liked (p. 471). Read this way, the pair differs in whether the upline's dealings with the member depended on the work, not in how much was given. Where they did, the member left and blames the upline (p. 479). Where they did not, he stayed, values the sponsor, and still does not do the work (p. 480). The second half is the inversion. The tie the paper counts as the strong one is printed beside none of the conduct a strong upline tie is supposed to bring about (the paper's claim at pp. 469–476). On this reading that tie holds because it did not depend on the work; it is what an idle member is left holding, and not a cause of anything he does. The tie in the passage on p. 479 is the ordinary, work-bound one, meeting a man it did not move.

Followed through Mark, the session prints three things happening, and a wanted possession for the downline is the slightest of them. First, Mark pursues his own wants: he points out a leather jacket, says he is interested in it himself, and arranges for the clerk to phone the author so that the author can buy it for him when it is reduced (p. 492); he asks about boot shops and goes to one although he knows the author has no interest in boots, and says his wife gets angry when he does this on such outings (p. 493). Second, Mark shows and coaches a manner: he takes control in the first shop, stumps a jeweller with knowledgeable questions (p. 492), tells the two downline that their ignorance of jewellery shows and that they should fake it, praises the author for walking straight in at the next shop, and says [6 words of Pratt (2000), p. 493] get treated well (p. 493). Third, Mark works the relationship and the business: he offers to pick up cheaper shorts near his home (p. 492), buys the author a biscuit with a father-and-son joke that the author returns, tells a salesperson the author will soon be rich or else Mark is wasting his time, and begins prospecting that salesperson (p. 493). Against this, the author records declining interest in men's jewellery (p. 492), little success in several clothing shops, being worn out (p. 493), and liking very few things all day, the jacket Mark had pointed out being one of them (p. 492). Mark's own stated view is that most people do not know what they want and learn it from watching the upline want things (p. 493). So in this exhibit what passes to the downline is mainly how Mark carries himself and a familial tie to Mark; the mentor relationship the paper places second is being built inside the practice it places first, and the standard set before the downline is the mentor more than any object. This sits close to what the author concedes on pp. 481–482, that the two kinds of practice blur as other distributors come to shape one's ideal self; it differs in holding that, in the one session printed, the blur is there from the first outing rather than arriving later.

Seekership is brought to Amway, not made by it. Members who identify, for or against, arrive already discontented with their job, money or family situation. Dream building gives that discontent a vocabulary rather than breaking a settled sense of self. Those who drift away are those whose outside lives were, or became, satisfactory. On this reading the first branch of the model sorts people by prior circumstance, not by whether a practice succeeded. The paper says identity deficits bite hardest on people in crisis or unhappy with who they are (p. 467). This concedes that prior state conditions the effect. The success-story distributor credits her upline with carrying her through a divorce (p. 470). The trouble predates the bond. Testimonies of an upline helping one member off drugs and feeding a couple in need (p. 471). Again need precedes attachment. In Table 1 the family dream is voiced by a man whose wife is worn out by her job and whose child is in day care all week (p. 465). The dream reads as a description of an existing strain. An ambivalent distributor frames his dream as escaping a job where others control whether he works (p. 480). This is a grievance about present employment. The non-renewer explains leaving by saying her job is now going well and she likes it (pp. 477–478). Deidentification here follows outside contentment. The general model adds a selection box and allows that some people are predisposed to seek, through dissatisfaction or disposition (p. 482). The paper thus names this route itself but does not test it on its own informants. Footnote 9 admits individual differences cannot be ruled out (p. 463). The design did not collect what would rule them out.

On a reading centered on engineered wanting, Amway first works on who a distributor is through dream building, before any mentor enters. Newcomers are taught to name a house, a child's lessons, or life without a boss as their own, so that what they lack becomes part of them. The present self, measured against that ideal, is found short—a loser's comfort zone—and the shortfall moves people to act. The push is kept from fading: an attained dream is traded for a larger one, and the most successful are shown starting over. Distributors' discontent is installed, not discovered, and dream building is the chief instrument unsettling the self. Anchors the reading: the paper proposes that Amway manufactures a nonreligious seekership, a discontent about who one is, and names dream building as the primary practice opening that gap — by binding the self to possessions, generating drives from the distance between current and ideal selves, and keeping those drives going (p. 464). Shows the installation step: possessions extend the self-concept, a needs analysis asks what one wants badly enough to do almost anything for, and Table 1 lists the concrete wants — a vast house, swimming lessons for a daughter, no boss — that newcomers learn to claim as their own (pp. 464–465). Delivers the shortfall: a hoped-for possession, once part of the self, reminds its holder of what she lacks and is not; the present self becomes a comfort zone or rut whose occupant is a loser, and the distance between that self and the dream is what drives action (p. 467). Supplies the renewal step: dream building does not end when a dream is reached — stopping is likened to a house left to decay, distributors are told to swap a realized dream for a bigger one and to keep climbing without peaking, and dreams drift toward larger, more abstract aims (p. 468). Confirms the renewal in distributors' own accounts: constant dream building kept members perpetually seeking self-validation, seekers treated dreams as standing motivators, and even the top distributor is described as starting anew all the time (p. 469).

The outcome is decided outside Amway, by how a member's existing circle responds when approached. Where family and friends join or at least tolerate the venture, the member's world fills with supporters and looks encapsulated. Where valued others recoil and the member is unwilling to lose them, the member hedges, hides and stalls. Where the member's confidants are hostile, the member turns against the organisation. Encapsulation is then something outsiders do to distributors as much as something positive programming does to members. Non-members told the author they avoid distributor friends and relatives, and a distributor calls the first months the hardest because of how intimates react (p. 474).
