The barrier is built from both sides. Bringing family and friends in is said to secure [6 words of Pratt (2000), p. 473] (p. 473). Who says yes determines the member's surroundings. A friend schedules his wedding against an Amway event, and unsupportive spouses are a named category needing continued persuasion (p. 472). Outsiders are active parties. One ambivalent distributor [6 words of Pratt (2000), p. 480] (p. 480). Another disowns Amway on the spot when a co-worker repeats a slur about it. The stalling follows an outsider's reaction. Ambivalent members restrict their calls to acquaintances outside daily life and agonise about exploiting close ties (p. 481). Footnote 16 has the author's own enthusiasm sagging around critical colleagues. Disidentified former members made sense of their experience with confidants who were firmly negative (p. 479). The valence of the outcome matches the valence of the audience.

Read the ruling-out as provisional. The paper prints that no current or former distributor interviewed gave a clear answer on net profit or loss (p. 463), and that informants disagreed on whether tapes, books and functions count as costs (p. 463). The one financial marker it names for the people it calls successful is [6 words of Pratt (2000), p. 463] (p. 463). What the two observations on p. 463 establish, then, is that identification type did not follow sales volume. Each informant's net position, and which way money moved between that informant and the people above them, is not observed for anyone. That unobserved quantity is what the printed disidentification material is about. One disidentified informant describes paying about $120 at his recruitment as the way out of a pressured sale (p. 479). The author's own summary of how disidentified distributors re-read upline warmth is that upline were being pleasant in order to make money for themselves (author's characterisation on p. 479). Members pay a fee of about $[7 words of Pratt (2000), p. 459] (p. 459). An upline tells a salesperson in the author's hearing that the author will be rich soon or the upline is wasting his time (p. 493), and the author reports that those above him cared only that he was selling and trying to sponsor (p. 460 n. 5). The wager is that the ending could go the other way on a narrower question: whether a member comes out as someone money flows from or someone money flows to may sort with the direction of their identification, and the comparison on p. 463 could not have detected it.

The concept is doing two jobs. X is a stated current dissatisfaction with one's own life; Y is excitement about a dream with no such dissatisfaction stated. The printed passages let them come apart. The author's own journal reports being caught up in a dream of personal freedom while also thinking the dreams foolish, and names nothing wrong with his present life (p. 466). A former distributor says they were excited at the beginning about their own business and financial independence and then lost interest (p. 477): Y occurred and lapsed, and X is not reported. The distributor who did not renew gives her reason as a present life she likes, a job that has reached the point of little overtime (p. 477): X is absent, and nothing is said about dreams. Where X is printed, the speaker ties it to paid work or to things lacked: a wife burned out at her job, two working parents and [6 words of Pratt (2000), p. 465] (p. 465); not wanting to be at the mercy of people at work (p. 480); not having what the recruiter had (p. 478). The wager is that X, not Y, is what goes with an identification of any kind forming, and that the printed passages show Y as what sessions, tapes and displays deliver while showing X in speakers' accounts of their jobs and households. If so, 'sensebreaking failed' on p. 477 covers two different things: excitement that was produced and faded, and a present life that was never, or no longer, found wanting.

The pair says the opposed leaver kept the wish for change and the detached one lost it. The passages on the opposed side do not line up that way. One former distributor was drawn by a successful member's large home because he lacked such possessions (p. 478) and describes becoming a lawyer as a dream worth hard work (p. 478): the wish is printed for him, and nothing about his upline is. The former distributor in the passage on p. 479 blames his upline for not recognizing the sales ability he came with and for relying on more meetings instead of finding a way to motivate him: no wish he was pursuing is printed, only a man who by his own telling still needed motivating. A third, whom the author files under the same opposed outcome, says he bought in only to get out of an embarrassing situation at a high-pressure presentation (p. 479); no passage gives him a dream. No passage says that the man of the passages on p. 478 is the man of the passage on p. 479. The upline tie does not separate the two sides either. By the author's account the detached formed no strong bonds with distributors (p. 478), and those who came to disidentify are reported with sparse and distant upline relationships (p. 479). The paper puts that weak tie after the loss of desire on the one side (p. 478) and before the opposition on the other (p. 479, the author's account); this reading puts it after on both. What the passages on p. 479 print, and the passage on pp. 477–478 does not, is a wrong: something done to the speaker by the people who brought him in or stood above him. The passage on pp. 477–478 has no Amway person in it; what changed was her regular job. The wager is that a leaver ends opposed when he carries such a wrong out with him, whether or not the wish for change survived, and ends detached when he carries none.

There is one practice, not two. The upline relationship does all the work, and dream building is something done inside it. Dreams are supplied, shaped and kept alive by the mentor, so a 'successful' dream is evidence of a working bond and a faded dream is evidence of a bond that never formed or went sour. The paper's two-by-two logic then collapses into a single dimension, the quality of the tie to the upline, with ambivalence as its middle value. Members learn what to dream mainly by modelling [6 words of Pratt (2000), p. 465] people in their own line (p. 465). The content of the dream comes from the upline. Upline and downline jointly craft the individual dream from a finite approved menu (p. 466). Dream building is described as a relational activity. In the appendix the Emerald chooses the shops, the colours and the items, and the author likes almost nothing all day (pp. 492–493). Meanwhile a joking father-son exchange occurs. The session produces a bond more visibly than a want. A distributor wants to reach Pearl in order to golf with his upline because he likes them (p. 471). The dream's object is the relationship. An interviewee says those who stay active are those who keep [7 words of Pratt (2000), p. 475] (p. 475). This is a member's own single-factor theory. The disidentified former distributor complains that his upline did not know how to excite him (p. 479). Failure to kindle the dream and failure of the bond are the same event in his telling. The deidentified leaver describes growing distance from his sponsors and discomfort with reverence for Diamonds (p. 478). The case filed under failed sensebreaking carries a relationship story. The paper acknowledges that the two kinds of tactic blur once sensegiving starts, as the ideal self comes under other distributors' influence (pp. 481–482).

The paper sets money aside too quickly. What it shows is not that finances are irrelevant but that members cannot or will not reckon them, and that the unreckoned items are precisely what flows up the line: tapes, books, functions, fees. Read this way, positive identification is the state of not having done the sum. Disidentification is the state of having done it and concluded that the warmth was commercial. Inactivity is the cheap holding position of paying only the renewal. The identification types are stances toward a ledger. No current or former distributor could, or would, state net profit, and they disagreed on whether training materials count as costs (p. 463). The paper reports this as a surprise and moves on. Here it is the central finding. The company's own figure for average monthly gross income of an active distributor is very low, and footnote 8 says nearly all actives fall short of high volume (p. 463). Most members are spending, not earning. Members pay a joining fee and often pay for books and tapes (p. 459). The costs are structural. Mentors direct which books to read and tapes to buy (p. 471). The sensegiver is also the person steering purchases. Disidentified members reinterpret upline kindness as a means to the upline's own income and feel used (p. 479). Their turn is an economic re-reading of the relationship. One former member recalls paying the entry sum as [6 words of Pratt (2000), p. 479] pressured pitch (p. 479). His grievance begins with a payment. Inactive distributors are defined as those who renew annually but do little else (p. 461). Every former distributor interviewed had left within a year, roughly when a first annual reckoning would fall due.
